# Four o’clock toast

At 21:00 on Saturday 7 November 2026, I started my last ever night shift in majors. At 07:30 on Sunday morning, I finished it.

From Monday, I move onto the days-only rota. After fourteen years of nights, I expected to feel uncomplicatedly pleased about this. Instead, I keep circling the subject like someone who has put something down and cannot remember where.

Every attempt to write about it has turned into either a eulogy or a complaint about the NHS. I do not want to write either. Night shifts were not a beloved dead relative, and I have written enough complaints. For fourteen years, nights were simply a large part of how I lived. The truth about them is less tidy than celebration or condemnation.

The move itself is practical. Partly it is my knees, partly my sleep, and partly the fact that my GP has made it clear that my blood pressure is not a joke any more. I am 42. There comes a point when treating your body as a badly maintained staff vehicle stops being funny, even to you.

My first night as an SHO was in 2012. During that first winter, I sat in my car at the Infirmary and cried because I could not remember whether I had given the second dose. I had. Everything had been done properly. My exhausted brain had simply declined to keep a reliable copy of events.

The detail that remains is the frost on the windscreen. I can still see it more clearly than I can remember the drive home. By then the dose was not the problem. The problem was that I had reached the point where even a completed task felt like an unresolved danger.

Nights taught me to check again, write things down and respect the moment when a tired brain stops being trustworthy. Useful lessons, but not cheap ones.

They also gave me something I have struggled to find anywhere else: the department at its most itself.

There are fewer managers around at night, less performance, less concern with how a thing might look from outside. This does not make night staff better than anyone else, and it certainly does not make the work easier. But people tend to become more honest about being stuck. They ask for help sooner. Kindness becomes practical rather than decorative.

People think nights are about adrenaline. Emergency medicine has its loud moments, of course, but adrenaline is a poor description of most of the work. Mostly, nights are about staying kind at five in the morning when you are empty.

Not extraordinarily kind. Not floating above the ward dispensing wisdom. Just remembering to explain something again without letting your impatience show. Noticing that somebody is frightened. Finding a form of words that does not make an already difficult moment worse. I have not always managed it. That is probably why I know it is a practice, not a personality trait.

Last winter, at around three in the morning, an elderly man held my hand and told me I had his daughter’s hands. There was no particular drama attached to it. He went home three days later.

I have thought about that small exchange far more than I would have expected. At three in the morning, kindness moves in both directions. Sometimes you go into a room thinking you are the one offering it and come out having been looked after yourself. That is not a lesson I would have chosen to learn at that hour, but I am glad I learned it.

And then there is the toast.

At four in the morning, somebody always makes toast in the staff room. Nobody admits to starting this. As far as I know, there was no meeting, no founding member and no agreed policy. It simply happens.

On a good night, it is a brief and cheerful interruption. On a difficult night, it is evidence that somebody has thought, however briefly, about everybody else. You can stand there for a few minutes with a piece of toast and not have to explain how the shift is going. Toast has never fixed a night shift. It has made a considerable number of them more bearable.

It would be convenient to say that these things made all the costs worthwhile, but I do not think life balances out that neatly.

Nights took sleep, then made sleep something I had to negotiate with even when I wasn’t working. They took ordinary time with people: the unremarkable evenings and weekends that do not look important on a rota but gradually turn out to be most of a life. My knees have views. My blood pressure has views. My GP has views, and is probably right.

Night shifts also kept me from both my nieces’ naming ceremonies. I saw what I could over video, which is better than nothing and not remotely the same as being there. My sister in Bangalore never once complained.

Her patience was kind, but it also made it easier for me to file those absences under “things that could not be helped”. Some of them really could not. The cost was still there, whether or not anybody sent me an invoice.

On Sunday morning, after handover, I drove home down London Road. The sun was coming up and I had the Radio 4 shipping forecast on catch-up, which is a gloriously impractical thing to listen to in Leicester. Somewhere in the middle of that calm recitation of weather happening elsewhere, I realised that I would not see that light from this side again.

I will see plenty more sunrises. I will drive down London Road again. But I will not be driving away from a night’s work into the start of everybody else’s Sunday, hollowed out and slightly wired, with the rest of the day already arranged around sleep.

That was when the change became real.

And yes, I am relieved. Enormously relieved. I am relieved at the prospect of sleeping when it is dark, of meals happening at recognisable meal times, of not having to work out which version of Tuesday I am currently living in. I am relieved that my body may stop having to make quite so many compensations.

I also feel like a traitor for being relieved.

Nobody has accused me of anything, to be clear. This is entirely home-grown. But nights are continuing without me. Other people will still be there at four in the morning, doing the work, making the tea and trying to remain human at five. A rota change is not desertion. I know this. It is possible to know something and still feel otherwise.

Folasade, our charge nurse on nights, is a useful corrective to any sentimental account I might construct. Folasade has done nights for twenty-two years and still beats me up the stairs. There is no romance in that, and no fragility either: just competence, stamina, and apparently a much better pair of knees.

So I will try not to build a monument to something that other people are still doing. Nights do not need one, least of all from someone who has just moved to days.

For the people still on them, my hopes are fairly modest. I hope Folasade keeps winning on the stairs. I hope that at four in the morning somebody still puts bread in the toaster, without announcement, and that people find their way into the staff room for a few minutes before going back out.

No speeches. No founder. No one taking credit. Just something warm, passed between tired people, repeated whenever it is needed.

Long may nobody own up.
